title: Soccerwise · Would you trust a robot referee?

slides.name: 1 · Teacher page

params.text:
Students decide where AI belongs in football, and what fair play means online.
Ten minutes. No phones, no join code: hands up, four corners and pair talk.
Every reveal is one click. Ask first, then press →.

slides.notes:
Themes from Youth Charter’s education packs. Our own copy, not their materials.

RUNNING ORDER
1 Cover — up as they come in
2 Scenario — 30s, read it, say nothing
3 Four corners — 90s, walk to a letter, one reason each
4 Pair talk — 75s
5 Did you know — 45s
6 Stand on the line — 2 min
7 Under the surface — 75s, one layer per click
8 Myth or fact — 2 min, the questions and answers
9 Three rules — 30s
10 Your choice — 45s

THE MOVE THAT MAKES IT WORK. Students hear each other before they hear you. After every vote, ask someone from a different corner to say the best reason for a corner they did not choose.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Use slide 3 as a show of hands. On slide 6, give each pair one card to place rather than standing.

EXTENSION. Design a pitch-side poster: one rule for fair play online.

slides.name: 2 · Would you trust a robot referee?

params.text: Would you trust a robot referee?

slides.notes: COVER. Up as the class comes in. Do not explain the question; let them start arguing about it in the doorway.

slides.name: 3 · The cameras say offside by a toenail. The whole stadium saw a goal.

params.text: The cameras say offside by a toenail. The whole stadium saw a goal.

slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 30 SECONDS. Read it once. Let it sit. Do not comment.

Most students will already have a VAR story. Save them for the next slide.

slides.name: 4 · Who should make the final call?

params.text: Who should make the final call?
It sees every millimetre, every time.
The AI checks. A person can overrule it.
Let the people on the pitch decide.

slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 90 SECONDS. Point to a corner of the room for each letter. Everyone moves; nobody sits this one out.

Then the key move: ask one person in each corner for their reason, and ask someone in ANOTHER corner to repeat it back fairly before they argue with it.

No right answer yet. C is closest to how it works today, but do not say so until slide 8.

slides.name: 5 · Statement · frame

params.text: Is a decision fair if it is accurate, but nobody can see how it was made?

slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 75 SECONDS. Pair with someone from a different corner.

The 75 seconds are the lesson. Resist filling them.

Listen for "but the computer can't be biased". That is the idea to test later: a system is only as fair as the people who built and use it.

slides.name: 6 · The ball is now a sensor

params.text: The ball is now a sensor
Points tracked on every player — 50 times a second at the 2022 World Cup
Readings a second from the ball — from a sensor inside the match ball
Goal-line technology at the World Cup — cameras check the whole ball crossed the line

params.label: Takeaway
params.text: Source: FIFA, semi-automated offside technology (Qatar 2022) and goal-line technology (Brazil 2014)

slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 45 SECONDS. Let them react to 500 a second. Then the point: the machine measures; the officials still decide.

Ask: does knowing this change your corner?

slides.name: 7 · Where should AI play?

params.text: Tracking how far each player runs
Flagging a player who needs rest
Choosing who gets a youth trial
The positions are arguable. That is the activity.

slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 2 MINUTES. STAND ON THE LINE. One wall is "AI can help", the opposite wall is "must stay human". Read each item before you reveal it; students stand where they think it goes. Then click to show where we put it.

The argument is always about the middle. Ask: "Which one did we put in the wrong place?"

The youth trial is the one to land: when AI helps decide who gets a chance, a hidden bias becomes someone's missed future.

slides.name: 8 · A video of a star player selling an app

params.text: A video of a star player selling an app
AI can learn how a player sounds
and make their mouth match the words
built to take your money or your data
their name used to trick their own fans
Check the player’s official channels before you believe or share.

slides.notes:
BEAT 6 · 75 SECONDS. Ask "what could be fake here?" before each click. Take their answers, then reveal the layer that matches.

The last layer is the point: deepfakes are not just a trick on you, they are harm to a real person. A hero uses their real voice; a fake steals it.

slides.name: 9 · Myth or fact?

params.text: The AI makes the offside decision
The officials decide. The technology draws the line.
It is both: steady running and all-out sprints.
Only famous people can be heroes
Anyone who speaks up for others can be one.
If a video looks real, it is real
AI can fake faces and voices. Check first.

slides.notes:
BEAT 7 · 2 MINUTES · QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS. Read each myth aloud. Thumbs up for true, thumbs down for false. Then click to show the fact.

Row 1 answers the four corners: today it is C, both.
Row 3: in 2020 Marcus Rashford spoke from his own childhood and won free school meals over the holidays. Ask who in their own community speaks up for others.

slides.name: 10 · Three rules for football in the age of AI

params.text: Three rules for football in the age of AI
In the order you would use them
No abuse of players, referees or fans, anywhere.
Official channels first. Fakes spread through kind people.
Keep humans in the big calls
AI can measure. People decide what is fair.

slides.notes: BEAT 8 · 30 SECONDS. One rule per click. Three is the limit; a fourth rule is one nobody remembers.

slides.name: 11 · Be the fair player

params.text: Decide one thing you will do this week to make football fairer, on the pitch or online.

slides.notes:
BEAT 9 · 45 SECONDS. Everyone decides one thing. A few volunteers say theirs aloud; the rest keep it.

If someone mentions online abuse they have seen, follow it up after the lesson.
